Polycarp on household and parish life

History and saints · Diognetus and Polycarp: Christian life

St. Polycarp on household and parish life

2 sectionsNot completed
Notes

St. Polycarp describes Christian responsibilities across households and the wider congregation. A presbyter is a church elder or minister addressed here as responsible for the community’s care. The letter brings family life, the position of widows, and leadership under a shared expectation of faithfulness and mercy.[1]

Faith within the household and community[1]

St. Polycarp connects resistance to greed with personal conduct and the upbringing of children. He describes faith, love, purity, and prayer as concerns for members of the household and for widows. His language about widows as God’s altar emphasizes the seriousness of their prayer and conduct in this letter.[1]

Read original passage

Various exhortations.

"But the love of money is the root of all evils." Knowing, therefore, that "as we brought nothing into the world, so we can carry nothing out," let us arm ourselves with the armour of righteousness; and let us teach, first of all, ourselves to walk in the commandments of the Lord. Next, [teach] your wives [to walk] in the faith given to them, and in love and purity tenderly loving their own husbands in all truth, and loving all [others] equally in all chastity; and to train up their children in the knowledge and fear of God. Teach the widows to be discreet as respects the faith of the Lord, praying continually for all, being far from all slandering, evil-speaking, false-witnessing, love of money, and every kind of evil; knowing that they are the altar of God, that He clearly perceives all things, and that nothing is hid from Him, neither reasonings, nor reflections, nor any one of the secret things of the heart.

What St. Polycarp expects of presbyters[1]

The ministers’ responsibilities include restoring those who wander, visiting the sick, and caring for widows, orphans, and the poor. St. Polycarp also rejects partiality, anger, greed, quick belief in accusations, and harsh judgment. Their awareness of their own need for forgiveness is part of his explanation of merciful leadership.[1]

Read original passage

The duties of presbyters and others.

And let the presbyters be compassionate and merciful to all, bringing back those that wander, visiting all the sick, and not neglecting the widow, the orphan, or the poor, but always "providing for that which is becoming in the sight of God and man;" abstaining from all wrath, respect of persons, and unjust judgment; keeping far off from all covetousness, not quickly crediting [an evil report] against any one, not severe in judgment, as knowing that we are all under a debt of sin. If then we entreat the Lord to forgive us, we ought also ourselves to forgive; for we are before the eyes of our Lord and God, and "we must all appear at the judgment-seat of Christ, and must every one give an account of himself." Let us then serve Him in fear, and with all reverence, even as He Himself has commanded us, and as the apostles who preached the Gospel unto us, and the prophets who proclaimed beforehand the coming of the Lord [have alike taught us]. Let us be zealous in the pursuit of that which is good, keeping ourselves from causes of offence, from false brethren, and from those who in hypocrisy bear the name of the Lord, and draw away vain men into error.

Scripture

1 Timothy 5:1–8

Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren;

The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.

Honour widows that are widows indeed.

But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.

Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.

But she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth.

And these things give in charge, that they may be blameless.

But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.

King James Version (1769), with Apocrypha · 1 Timothy 5:1–8[2]
